children: By Mike O'Sullivan
France's political class has never been known for its financial literacy, but it may be hitting a new low.

Wild suggestions that France should just cancel its central bank's debt, now running at recessionary levels, are being aired in the French media. "All we have to do," far-left politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon said in June, is take that debt and "chuck it in the fire."
The belief that debt could be magicked away rather than corrected with fiscal discipline comes with dangerous consequences.
Bond markets are offering a preview.

Ten-year French government bond yields have risen a full percentage point over the past few months, hitting their highest level since 2008, 4.2%, this week. Sovereign debt yields in other major economies, including the U.S., Japan, Italy, Canada, and the United Kingdom, are also hitting or surpassing levels last seen around the 2008-09 financial crisis. Stubbornly elevated inflation is a factor, as are these governments' gargantuan fiscal deficits.
Yet, in none of these countries has a credible politician stood up to fix the situation.

At the end of last week, a large French business network gathered in Paris' Roland Garros stadium to hear the front-runners in the coming presidential election discuss their economic policies, including how to address France's massive deficit. Roland Garros, with its sleek architecture, red clay courts, and private terraces, is one of the more stylish and elegant parts of the city, and not a bad location to discuss finance and economics.
Unfortunately, France's political elites disappointed.

Mélenchon and his far-right counterpart, Marine Le Pen, appeared to treat the event as a lighthearted, postholiday chat show, not a forum to debate the fault line that could pitch the euro zone into another debt crisis. (To be fair, the European Central Bank, which should be a figure of authority in this conversation, hasn't shown much concern, either).

Though France's presidential election is still months away, American and international investors need to pay close attention to it, both as a specific risk factor for bonds, foreign exchange, and equities, and as a harbinger of what might befall other major economies.

If, for instance, both Melenchon and Le Pen make it through to the second round of the presidential election, bond investors might desert France. Capital flight will become a risk, French bank shares will collapse, luxury goods firms will become bargains, and the euro will likely fall. Bond investors will rush to the few havens the euro zone still offers-Germany, the Netherlands, and Ireland, as well as assets in periphery countries like Norway and Switzerland.

More broadly, a continued rise in French yields in the face of policy inaction (a draft budget is to be presented to parliament at the end of September), might, for the first time in more than a decade, sensitize international investors to the credit risk inherent in government balance sheets.

France's situation is particularly instructive for the U.S. because the two countries share several things in common. Both have budget deficits around 5%, a level historically associated with wartime or a recession. Their debt-to-GDP ratios are both on course to surpass 120% in coming years, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Much of that government spending goes to social welfare programs, such as healthcare and pensions, that don't produce large growth gains. And both lack the political appetite to correct their fiscal situations with tax hikes or spending cuts.
Congress hasn't even hinted it will look into addressing the $40 trillion debt load. The Trump administration is holding steadfast to the "we can grow ourselves out of this" line.

Having witnessed firsthand the brutal effect of a debt crisis and the subsequent austerity on the Irish economy from 2010 onward, my sense is that most French and American policymakers are badly underpricing what may result from their inaction.
Bond yields will keep going up. That means that in some of the richest countries on Earth, life will become more expensive for everyday people. The quality of life they can afford will drop.
Eventually, the debt issue will eclipse all other economic or political concerns.

In that way, France's changing status from a core safe-haven bond market to a peripheral one is a signal of a coming debt purgatory for developed countries-a long period where indebtedness dominates markets, domestic policymaking, and geopolitics.
